question: What evidence shows that autonomous research agents outperform a single well-prompted model on difficult technical research tasks?
count_note: web_calls counts search-service invocations; search_queries counts submitted queries; opened_pages counts all open operations including repeat line reads and one failed HTML open (7 distinct successful pages, 1 failed URL).

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.support: Inspected lines 29–35: Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 workers reportedly improved 90.2% over single Opus 4 on an internal research evaluation; token use explains much performance variation. Chats, single agents and teams consume approximately 1:4:15 tokens.
sources.limitations: Internal evaluation lacks public sample-level outcomes, uncertainty and equal-budget controls. Breadth-first web research differs from experimental science.

sources.title: AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation
sources.support: Inspected results, limitations and ablations: 24 BioML tasks, mean leaderboard percentile 74.40 versus Autoresearch 66.07; matched model, interface and experimental hardware. Component ablations improve all four listed tasks. Authors explicitly acknowledge additional LLM tokens.
sources.limitations: Experimental compute is matched, total inference cost is not. Aggregate standard errors are 6.20 and 7.38; they do not establish paired significance. Comparison against other published agents uses modified hardware.

sources.title: ST-Bench: A Spatial-Temporal Benchmark for Multi-Agent System Generation on Scientific Research Tasks
sources.support: Inspected setup and results: 100 Earth science tasks, 492 held-out queries; same GPT-5 backbone. Composite score 32.0 for strongest workflow versus 11.0 for single agent. Most improvement is reaching numerical output; conditional metric quality is comparable. Inference time is about 4.5 times baseline.
sources.limitations: Comparator explicitly described as GPT-5 one-turn. Workflow optimization and larger inference budget confound architecture. Token accounting incomplete; numerical sanity is not comprehensive scientific validation.

sources.title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
sources.support: Inspected v3 methods, conclusion and uncertainty tables: 260 configurations across six benchmarks, matched reasoning budgets and tools. Reported gains span +80.8% on Finance Agent to −70.0% on PlanCraft; diminishing coordination returns near 45% single-agent success.
sources.limitations: Threshold is empirical within tested domains. Technical benchmark extensions use only 20 instances each with wide intervals. Version-dependent: original abstract reports 180 configurations; v3 reports 260.

sources.title: Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
sources.support: Inspected Table 1: at 2,000 requested thinking tokens, averaged SAS accuracy is .421 versus .389 sequential and .403 debate. At 100 tokens, averages favor several teams. Authors diagnose imperfect Gemini budget accounting.
sources.limitations: World-knowledge question answering, not end-to-end scientific research. Requested and actual tokens can differ. Individual model/dataset cells include exceptions, so title is too broad if read literally.

sources.title: ResearchClawBench: A Benchmark for End-to-End Autonomous Scientific Research
sources.support: Inspected abstract: seven research agents and seventeen native LLMs using ResearchHarness; strongest reported agent 21.5 versus strongest harness LLM 20.7. Main failures include protocol and evidence mismatch.
sources.limitations: Only abstract was inspectable; full HTML failed. Different system/model maxima cannot identify causal benefit, and 0.8 points has no inspected significance estimate.

sources.title: An Empirical Study of Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Research
sources.support: Inspected experimental setup: nanochat-style optimization with GLM workers, RTX 3090 and 300/600-second training constraints. Parallel subagents improve early; teams diversify architectural changes but incur crashes and deliberation overhead.
sources.limitations: Narrow optimization task, mixed model roles and no inspected statistical uncertainty. Matching training time does not ensure equal LLM budgets.

claims.text: There is positive task-specific evidence for agent teams, especially computational experimentation and broad research, but no inspected evidence establishes universal superiority over an optimized single model with equal total resources.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate confidence in conditional benefits; low confidence in general superiority.

claims.text: AutoScientists offers the most directly relevant inspected comparison: +8.33 leaderboard-percentile points on 24 biomedical ML tasks against a single research agent with matched experimental compute.
claims.uncertainty: Independent reproduction and equal-inference comparison remain unverified.

claims.text: ST-Bench shows higher composite performance but mainly more completed analyses; comparison to one-turn GPT-5 does not settle the well-prompted iterative single-agent challenge.
claims.uncertainty: Higher score need not imply deeper scientific insight.

claims.text: Anthropic's 90.2% improvement is a relative internal-evaluation report, not a 90.2-percentage-point gain or an equal-cost causal estimate.
claims.uncertainty: Absolute scores and sampling uncertainty unavailable.

claims.text: Compute-controlled comparisons show teams can help decomposable tasks and hurt sequential tasks; stronger individual agents frequently erase coordination benefits.
claims.uncertainty: Transfer to novel technical research is uncertain.

claims.text: Current end-to-end research scores are low; agent branding alone supplies little evidence of superiority.

contradictions.issue: Large gains coexist with equal-budget regressions.
contradictions.resolution: Different tasks, comparator strength and compute accounting explain much of the apparent conflict; do not pool percentages.

contradictions.issue: Nearly threefold composite gain coexists with similar conditional scientific metric quality.
contradictions.resolution: Coverage drives most gain; distinguish completion from quality.

contradictions.issue: Title suggests general single-agent dominance, but table includes team wins at small budgets.
contradictions.resolution: Report budgets and exceptions; avoid converting a trend into a universal claim.

contradictions.issue: Search abstract has 180 configurations but inspected v3 has 260.

conclusion: The strongest defensible answer is conditional: autonomous agent teams can improve exploration and experiment selection on difficult, decomposable technical tasks. Evidence is weaker that architecture itself beats a carefully prompted, tool-equipped, iterative single model when inference cost, experiments, tools and time are matched. Treat broad superiority claims as unproven.
followups: Run paired, repeated trials on held-out technical research tasks using the same model, sources, tools and starting artifacts.
Compare a tuned single agent, a single agent with self-critique and memory, independent sampling with selection, and coordinated teams; this separates workflow, search and coordination benefits.
Report two resource regimes: equal total dollars/tokens/experimental compute and equal wall-clock time with parallelism allowed.
Blind expert grading of correctness, novelty, reproducibility, evidence-to-claim alignment and intervention burden; retain runnable artifacts and failed trajectories.
Publish paired confidence intervals, prompt-tuning budgets, contamination controls and task-level failures; reproduce the strongest scientific study independently.
